session.name: Welcome and Opening Keynote of MLcon Berlin 2026
session.details: Welcome and Opening Keynote of MLcon Berlin 2026 by the program chair Sebastian Meyen.

session.longAbstract:
Topics covered include:

  • Designing APIs that can be reliably understood and consumed by AI agents

  • Improving API descriptions and semantic metadata for machine-driven discovery

  • Using OpenAPI to create machine-readable contracts that support agent interactions

  • Applying Overlay specifications to enrich and govern existing APIs without redesigning them

  • Modeling deterministic workflows with Arazzo for repeatable and controlled automation

  • Implementing fine-grained authorization and policy enforcement for autonomous agents

  • Creating safe experimentation environments through sandboxing strategies

  • Building governance frameworks that balance automation with operational control

  • Establishing API design patterns that minimize ambiguity and reduce agent errors

Throughout the workshop, participants will work on real-world scenarios where AI agents consume APIs across multiple systems and services. They will design API contracts, define workflow specifications, apply governance controls, and evaluate how different design decisions influence agent behavior.

By the end of the session, attendees will have a practical toolkit for making existing API landscapes AI-ready. They will leave with proven design patterns, governance templates, and architectural guidance that can be applied immediately to enterprise API programs without requiring a complete platform redesign.

Whether you are an API architect, platform engineer, integration specialist, or technology leader, this workshop will help you prepare your API ecosystem for a future where autonomous agents become first-class API consumers.
session.name: Workshop: Intentional API Design: Build APIs that Deliver Value to Humans and AI Agents
session.details:
Design APIs that truly serve their purpose — deliberately and effectively. In this workshop, you'll learn how to design APIs not just correctly, but intentionally — with a strong focus on stakeholder needs (AI agents and humans), usability, and long-term maintainability. Move beyond ad-hoc decisions and start crafting APIs as products that offer real value to both internal and external consumers.
Modern software architecture increasingly relies on well-designed APIs. Yet, too often, APIs are built without a clear understanding of who uses them, what they expect, and how design decisions affect long-term usability and maintenance. This workshop addresses the gap between building APIs right and building the right APIs. We explore the philosophy of Intentional API Design — the practice of making every design decision consciously and deliberately. You’ll learn to approach APIs not as mere technical interfaces, but as products shaped by business needs, user expectations, and architectural constraints.
Workshop Outline Block 1: Understanding API Stakeholders and Their Needs (AI Agents as a Stakeholder) Block 2: Intentional Design Principles Block 3: Frontend and Backend API Design Block 4: API Lifecycle and Iteration

Beyond Single-Agent: Designing Multi-Agent Systems Around Failure Modes
session.details: Most multi-agent systems fail because they parallelize work without understanding how individual agents fail. This session turns modern benchmark error taxonomies—execution, coherence, and verification—into an architectural lens. We present a conceptual architecture where roles are matched to failure profiles: Planners maintain intent, Scouts gather information, Specialized Workers act, and Independent Verifiers challenge assumptions. Attendees will leave with a design checklist for building resilient agent stacks that allow coordination to genuinely outperform raw model capability, backed by insights from SOTA results on ARC-AGI-2 and Deep Research Bench.

session.name: Break
Your Enterprise RAG Has No Legal Basis
session.details: Your RAG system works beautifully. Under GDPR, it has no legal basis to exist. Clean architecture. Proper embeddings. Maybe even agentic tool calling. You followed best practices. But when the auditor asks “what’s the legal basis for this processing?” there’s no answer. General-purpose “ask anything” chatbots have no defined purpose. Without a defined purpose, no legal basis can exist under GDPR. The architecture itself is the violation. In this talk, we’ll live-code a “best practices” enterprise knowledge bot, then ask the questions nobody asks: Where is purpose limitation enforced? Where is legal basis documented? I’ll show why anonymization doesn’t save you. 97% accuracy isn’t “anonymous” under GDPR. It’s still PII. Then I’ll show you the fix: a purpose-scoped bot architecture where legal basis is a first-class configuration item. Each bot gets a defined purpose, scoped data access, configured tools, and documented legal basis. The architecture enforces the boundaries. The retrieval layer can only access documents within that bot’s scope. Non-compliance becomes architecturally impossible. The good news? You didn’t waste your investment. This is a 50k governance layer, not a rewrite.

session.name: Embodied AI: Vision-Language Models Meet Physical Systems
session.details: Vision-language models are rapidly moving beyond digital tasks into systems that must perceive, decide, and act in the physical world. But this shift introduces an entirely different class of engineering challenges. In this talk, we explore hybrid architectures that combine the contextual reasoning of VLMs and VLAs with deterministic control loops, addressing the fundamental tension between the flexibility of neural inference and the hard timing guarantees required by physical actuators. We cover real-time visual perception on edge hardware, predictive models for latency-critical scenarios, and practical strategies for maintaining human-interpretable decision layers in autonomous systems. Drawing from use cases in active tracking, precision actuation, and autonomous navigation, we share where multimodal models genuinely add value over classical approaches — and where they don't.

session.name: Break
Avoid data leakage in Agentic RAG by using ReBAC
session.details:
We’ve recently seen the rise of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. With the proliferation of AI Agents & LLMs in Enterprise, the next step in the evolution is Agentic RAG. But this introduces a subtle but critical problem: authorization is no longer a single check, but a chain of decisions across tools, memory, and retrieval layers and this breaks more often than you expect.
This talk is a deep dive into how modern authorization systems can ensure that AI Applications have access only to authorized data. The talk will look at why the Google Zanzibar model of authorization which uses Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC) is well suited to handle dynamic, relationship-driven authorization at scale. The talk explains how the Google Zanzibar system works under the hood, and how to apply it to Agentic RAG with techniques such as pre-filteration and post-filteration. Learning these fundamentals might just prevent broken access control issues in your application.
The talk will also include a live coding demo implementing authorization for Agentic RAG using Open Source tools such as Weaviate, Langchain, and SpiceDB.

session.name: Building agent interfaces: designing for a user that is a machine
session.details: Increasingly the user of your software is not a human, it is an agent: one that decides in milliseconds, can be wrong, and that you cannot blindly trust. The common mistake is treating that agent as just a faster API client. It is not. It is its own kind of user, with its own strengths and bottlenecks, and agent experience is now part of your user experience. Drawing on real lessons from shipping tools that agents use every day, this talk walks through four engineering concerns that change when your user is a machine, each with a practical technique and an honest story of getting it wrong first: token usage and how to measure the real cost of a successful outcome, error recovery and self-healing, tool discoverability and why so many tool descriptions go unused, and trust boundaries, where the same capability needs a different security model depending on where it runs. The principles apply to any tool, API, or agent platform you build.

session.name: Model as Code: Code-Driven Model Development for Intelligent Apps with Small LLMs
session.details: AI-assisted development is transforming how we write software, but what if we applied the same software engineering rigor to the models themselves? In this talk, we introduce Model as Code: a practical, code-first approach to building intelligent applications where models become first-class, inspectable, testable, and composable citizens of the codebase. Instead of treating AI as opaque API black boxes, we define, configure, evaluate, version, and evolve models directly in code using familiar developer workflows, Git, CI/CD, and automated testing. We’ll explore how small language models and lightweight neural components can be deeply integrated into production applications when privacy, latency, cost, and on-device execution matter. Expect a hands-on, developer-centric journey: from describing model behavior in code, to connecting models with tools and context, safely evaluating changes, and iterating with confidence. The goal is to turn AI development from prompt magic into reliable engineering. Attendees will leave with a clear mental model and immediately applicable patterns for building AI-native applications where code, models, and agents evolve together.

session.workshopRequirements:
Built for developers who already code with AI and want to ship with confidence.

  • Developers using AI to write code, from autocomplete to command-line agents

  • Builders who ship quickly but haven't yet learned spec-driven or autonomous development

  • Tech leads who want a repeatable, tool-agnostic way for a team to trust AI-written code

Requirements: a laptop and the AI coding tool you already use (for example Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code or OpenCode). No prior spec-driven or autonomous-development experience needed.
session.longAbstract:
Day 2: Guardrails You Build Yourself

Turn a working app into one you'd actually deploy.

You will work on:

  • Mapping the "certainty ladder": an instruction the agent might follow, versus a check that runs every time whatever wrote the code

  • Choosing what earns your trust in a commit, then turning each one into an enforced check

  • Building your own preflight check by working with your AI tool - the lasting skill is making guardrails, not being handed them

  • Enforcing checks across the whole codebase, and holding the agent to your standard — no self-granted exceptions, no "good enough"

  • Using an AI agent to review for design issues like duplicated logic and weak structure

  • Optional advanced step: pointing an adversarial agent at your own app, as one more check you can build

Focus:
The guardrails are what let you ship code you didn't read line by line — and you leave with a portable setup you can drop into any repository.
session.name: Agentic Software Engineering Bootcamp Day 2: From Spec to Production-Ready Software
session.details:
Your AI assistant wrote the feature. The tests pass. It looks correct. But you didn't read every line, so how do you know it does what you meant? Maybe the model got it right the first time. Maybe not. From where you sit, those two outcomes look identical. That uncertainty, not the quality of any one tool, is the real distance between "I built something" and "I can put this in production."

This hands-on, two-day workshop closes that distance. Day one is about aim: build fast and loose, hit the moment the assistant confidently produces something other than what you intended, and learn that the specification, not the code, was always the hard part. You'll leave with an app that does what you actually meant.

Day two is about confidence. You'll build your own pre-commit checks for quality, security, dependency vulnerabilities, and your own design standards, and wire them into a gate that blocks bad commits across the whole codebase.

For developers who already code with AI and want to move from "it works on my machine" to "I'd put my name on this." Bring a laptop and the AI tool you already use.

session.longAbstract:
The workshop covers the areas of software development where AI can deliver real, immediate value to your team’s existing practices:

∙ Planning and Processes — using AI to design systems, surface tradeoffs, and stress-test proposals before you commit to them

∙ Code Review — catching logic errors, security gaps, and edge cases, and learning to interpret and push back on AI suggestions intelligently

∙ Debugging — a systematic approach to giving AI the right context, generating hypotheses, and getting to root causes faster

∙ Upgrades & Routine Tasks — tackling dependency upgrades, migrations, refactoring, and test generation with repeatable, AI-powered workflows

The workshop includes hands-on exercises using real code and real problems. Participants leave with concrete techniques and ideas to implement back in their teams. The workshop assumes users have access to at least one robust AI agent platform. This workshop is designed for technical audiences who work on software. No hype, no generic AI intros — just practical skills that transfer directly to your daily work.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
session.name: The Augmented Engineer [Onsite Only]
session.details: Most engineers have used AI to write code. Far fewer have used it for the work that actually fills their week like designing systems, pressure-testing assumptions, navigating incidents, synthesizing decisions, understanding unfamiliar codebases, and keeping institutional knowledge from evaporating into Slack threads. This full-day, hands-on workshop teaches software engineers and adjacent roles how to use AI as an adversarial thinking partner across the full range of engineering work. Participants learn to make AI argue against their designs, surface what they missed in a plan, find the root cause hiding behind a red herring, triage communication noise, and build reusable workflows that stick beyond the workshop itself. The day runs over a dozen blocks covering agent setup, context artifact creation, communication and connector workflows, visual design, research and decision-making, code review and threat modeling, incident response, documentation, and team evaluation — culminating in on-demand dashboards that surface how a team's time and effort is actually being spent. All instruction is tool-agnostic. Participants bring their own AI tool. The majority of each block is hands-on practice on realistic scenarios, with three consistent debrief questions that build the habit of treating AI output as a starting point, not an answer.

session.workshopRequirements:
Is this training for you?

  • Engineers: Looking to move past the hype and harden their terminal-based AI workflow.

  • Tech-Adjacent Professionals: (PMs, Architects, Technical Founders) Who are comfortable with basic terminal navigation, Git basics, and configuration files, and want to build or prototype at lightning speed without a full engineering team.
session.longAbstract:
What We’ll Cover:

  • Architectural Control: Mastering Plan Mode for safe, multi-step reasoning before a single line of code changes.

session.name: The Terminal is Your Canvas: Professional Vibe Coding with Claude Code
session.details:
Forget copy-pasting from a browser tab. If you’re still using Claude through a standard chat window, you’re leaving massive velocity on the table.
Claude Code brings Anthropic’s most powerful models directly into the terminal, executing complex, multi-step tasks natively inside a codebase or project directory. But going from "cool tool" to a predictable, production-grade workflow requires strategy.
This intensive, one-day training is built for anyone who wants to master autonomous orchestration, safely manage multi-file mutations, and scale their output without losing control. While designed with software engineering patterns, this training is highly accessible to non-engineers with a strong technical foundation (e.g., technical product managers, solutions architects, data analysts, or technical founders) looking to bridge the gap between idea and execution.
The Ultimate Claude Masterclass
This isn't a surface-level overview. By the end of this intensive day, you will know everything there is to know about Claude. From its underlying cognitive architecture and advanced prompting behaviors to its deepest terminal configurations, hidden flags, and agentic limits—you will leave with a complete, 360-degree understanding of Anthropic's ecosystem.

Key Skills You Will Master:

  • Agentic Orchestration: Directing autonomous AI agents to perform multi-step, multi-file operations safely.

  • Context Engineering: Structuring project documentation and constraints so AI tools perfectly understand your domain.

  • Workflow Automation: Building reusable custom skills, slash commands, and automated CI/CD pipelines.

  • Modern Git Topology: Managing isolated development branches using Git worktrees to run parallel AI sessions without breaking your main workspace.

  • Ecosystem Integration: Connecting LLMs to external data sources, APIs, and local developer tools using the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

session.details:
In this hands-on workshop, you will learn how to design, secure, and govern MCP servers, enabling trusted connectivity between AI models, agents, and enterprise systems.

Looking to accelerate AI adoption while maintaining control over security, governance, and data?
Need to connect applications, APIs, and enterprise data to AI agents and new business use cases?
Are you looking to scale up your AI projects, secure interactions with models, orchestrate data flows, and ensure your architectures are compliant?

This TechLab is for you!

session.name: Spec Driven Development: The End of Vibe coding
session.details:
Developers now create entire applications by simply chatting with AI tools. More and more startups rely on predominantly AI-generated code. But what initially thrilled developers quickly leads to frustration: generic code, poor architecture, and security vulnerabilities.

In this talk, I demonstrate how Spec Driven Development (SDD) solves these problems. Instead of coding first and documenting later, SDD begins with precise specifications as the "single source of truth." Various tools and CLIs make this methodology practically applicable today with a structured 4-phase approach: Specify, Plan, Tasks, Implement.

Using a real project, I show how SDD works with modern AI coding tools. I share honest insights from hands-on experience: where SDD excels, where it fails, and whether the specification overhead actually leads to better results.

Attendees will learn when SDD makes sense, which tools are available, how to integrate this methodology into existing workflows, and why structured AI development could shape the future.

Key takeaways: Practical SDD implementation, tool ecosystem overview, real-world examples, and critical evaluation of specification-driven AI development.

session.name: Build a private cluster for the office
session.details:
For almost three years now John has been building private (local, shared server, private data room and private cloud) systems for his customers, mostly financial institutions, large banks, but also legal, medical and government work. Most of these organisations simply can't use the frontier models, even if hosted in the EU. It's not just cost, it's the need for long-term support, SLAs, total privacy, ownership, accountability, governance, repeatability, the list goes on... There's Bedrock and Vertex from Amazon and Google, and companies like RunPod with EU instances, but renting 24/7 costs roughly half the hardware's purchase price every month.

For an office of about 10–50 people, not coders, a small redundant cluster of Mac Minis or Studios, NVIDIA DGX Sparks or even both are perfect for the job, dedicated or shared. John will start with setting up the machines, what needs networking and what doesn't, which models work best, adding tools and access to local data feeds, even private ones. He'll also cover KV-cache loading from SSD for near-instant document access to replace RAG. These models can code but that's not the main goal here, it's for private internal and customer data.

This will be a technical talk but you will walk away with enough knowledge to start replacing your team's dependence on OpenAI, Anthropic and other frontier models. Open-weight models all the way.

session.name: Hybrid ML Systems: When to Use Rules, Small Models, and LLMs in Production
session.details:
Rules, small models, or LLMs? In production, defaulting to "just use an LLM" is often the wrong call. Knowing when it's the right one is the actual skill.

Using a production NLP pipeline that processes millions of receipts across diverse formats and languages, this talk gives a practical framework for hybrid ML architectures. We cover when rules still win on cost, latency, and auditability. We cover when a small, purpose-trained model is the right fit for high-volume extraction. And we cover when an LLM's flexibility justifies its cost, for example on long-tail layouts, ambiguous entity resolution, or adapting to new formats without retraining.

We'll share concrete integration patterns: LLMs as fallback handlers, as rule and training-data generators, and as error evaluators. We'll also walk through the cost, latency, and reliability trade-offs each brings, and what broke when we got the boundaries wrong.

You'll leave with a decision framework for combining rules, small models, and LLMs in production, instead of picking just one.

session.name: From Lab to Production: Making Computer Vision Systems Work in the Real World
session.details:
Most Computer Vision projects don't fail because of poor code; they fail when they enter production. In the lab, 99% accuracy is a triumph. Inproduction, that same model can become an undeployable liability due to data drift, concept drift, 5G connectivity gaps, or even simply overheating hardware.

In this session, we move past the MLOps hype to explore a 5-step framework designed for B2B developers to bridge the gap between a "golden dataset" and a stable production architecture. We will walk through the critical decision matrix of task selection, map model architectures to hardware constraints (from NVIDIA Jetson to
Cloud-native), and discuss why the "Art" of AI lies in the long-term operations lifecycle. Attendees will leave with a practical checklist to ensure their next CV project ripens like fine wine rather than turning into "Day 2" technical debt.

session.name: From Demos to Durable Agents: Engineering the Reliability Stack for Production
session.details:
Everyone can build an AI agent demo in a weekend, but shipping one that works reliably in a 24/7 high-stakes environment—like institutional finance or crypto market intelligence—is a massive engineering challenge. This session moves past the "vibe coding" hype to dive into the hard-technical "Reliability Stack" required to turn fragile LLM scripts into durable, production-ready systems.
Drawing from firsthand experience building research and trading agents at a leading blockchain analytics firm (Nansen), I will detail the architectural patterns used to solve the "Agentic Loop" problem. Key topics include:
State-Machine Orchestration: Moving from simple RAG to structured state machines to prevent reasoning loops.
Non-Deterministic Evaluation: Implementing "LLM-as-a-Judge" frameworks and semantic unit testing to quantify performance.
The Reliability Stack: Deploying guardrails, circuit breakers, and "Reasoning Trace" observability to debug autonomous failures in real-time.
Governance in Finance: Building audit trails and decision boundaries that satisfy both users and compliance.
Attendees will leave with a practical framework for evaluating agent readiness and a checklist of failure modes that only appear at scale.

session.name: Beyond Commercial Monoliths: How to Build a Vendor-Agnostic Invoice Extraction Pipeline with S(V)LMs and Visual Judging
session.details: Relying entirely on monolithic commercial Vision APIs for document processing introduces significant enterprise risks, including unpredictable costs, model deprecations, and silent updates. This presentation delivers a hands-on architectural analysis of a resilient alternative for scanned multi-page commercial invoices. We demonstrate how self-hosted, open-weights Small (Vision) Language Models (S(V)LMs) can be leveraged as a sovereign foundation for layout-aware, template-independent field extraction. To mitigate failures caused by document complexity—such as fragmented tables—we introduce a decoupled validation layer: self-hosted S(V)LMs perform the heavy lifting of data extraction, while Gemini 3.0 Flash is integrated strictly as a final visual judge. Auditing structured output against the original image eliminates vendor lock-in. Attendees will leave with a practical blueprint for building production-grade pipelines that ensure measurable extraction quality while maintaining architectural control and long-term cost stability.

session.name: Build Your Own MCP Server and Develop AI Agents from Scratch
session.details: In this full-day hands-on workshop, participants learn how to develop their own MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers and use them to build powerful AI agents that can access external tools and data sources. From the basics of the MCP protocol to production-ready implementation—with plenty of hands-on experience and real-world use cases. Participants will gain in-depth insights into the architecture of the Model Context Protocol and develop their own MCP servers step by step. Through practical exercises and realistic scenarios, they will learn how to create AI agents that can interact seamlessly with different systems and data sources.

session.name: Voice Agents - Where Latency Hides and How to Fight It
session.details: A voice agent pipeline looks simple: speech-to-text, LLM, text-to-speech. In practice, most of the engineering effort goes into things that aren't on that diagram. This talk breaks down the latency budget of a real-time voice agent and what has to happen between the user going silent and the agent starting to speak. I'll cover the parts that took us the longest to get right: detecting when someone actually stopped talking (harder than it sounds), streaming orchestration when components in your pipeline run at different speeds, handling interruptions without losing conversation context, and transport layer choices that affect how responsive the whole thing feels. I'll go through specific patterns we landed on as well as what didn't work and architectural choices we had to adapt. We'll also evaluate the newer speech-to-speech models and analyze their pros and cons for production deployments. If you're a developer who might end up building anything voice-based in the next time, this is the context you'll wish you had going in.

session.name: When Your Only Tool Is An LLM-Hammer…
session.details:
…you try and solve every problem with a prompt.

When the term "AI" is used these days, it usually refers only to LLMs. Yet especially in the field of deep learning, there are many other exciting and important developments that you should be aware of if you want to integrate AI features into your software. In this session, we will establish initial guidelines to answer the following questions that are fundamental to project success:

* When do I need an LLM? When do I need other models?

* If I need an LLM: which one?

* Where do I find such models and how do I choose the right one?

* When do I need to train my own model, and when is an off-the-shelf solution sufficient?

* What is the right way to integrate a model into my software?

Knowing the answers to these questions will help you prevent many painful and expensive mistakes that most “AI” projects run into these days.

session.name: Teaching Machines to See and Read: The Science and Applications of Multimodal AI
session.details: Multimodality represents one of AI's most fascinating and business-actionable frontiers, yet its potential remains largely untapped. In this session, we'll explore multimodal architectures from CLIP to cutting-edge VLMs, discovering practical use cases where multimodal AI delivers real business value.

session.name: Your AI Demo Is Great. Your AI Bill Is Not.
session.details: Building Cost-Effective Systems in the Era of Expensive AI The era of “just throw an LLM at it” is ending. As AI companies raise prices, move toward IPOs, and optimize for profitability, teams are being forced to rethink how they build AI-powered products. Cost is no longer just an infrastructure concern; it is now a product, architecture, and business strategy problem. In this session, we’ll explore how to design AI systems that are useful, reliable, and cost-effective. We’ll look at where costs actually come from, including model calls, context size, retrieval, orchestration, evaluation, and unnecessary agentic complexity. We’ll discuss practical patterns for reducing spend: using smaller models where possible, caching, routing, prompt and context optimization, open-source models, hybrid architectures, and moving away from vendor lock-in. Attendees will leave with a framework for deciding when to use proprietary APIs, when to move to open-source models, and how to evaluate whether an AI feature is delivering real ROI.

session.name: The Last App: When Software Stops Being a Product
session.details:
For forty years, an app was a product. You built it once and shipped one version to everyone. That era is ending, not because software is disappearing, but because it is splitting in two.

On one side is the "every-app": one AI system that builds whatever you need, shaped to you. Your own budget tracker, your own tools, summoned in a sentence, never finished. This doesn't reduce the software in the world. It multiplies it.

On the other side is what the every-app can't replace. It is the most valuable software there is. Some exists so a company has someone to blame when it fails. Some matters only because everyone else is already on it. Some operates where a confident wrong answer is a disaster: payments, healthcare, anything regulated. The every-app takes the easy middle. The hard, valuable edges remain.

We've climbed this ladder before: code, then builds, then directing AI. Each step traded typing for judgement. This is the next step. It won't be painless, but the lasting skill was never owning a safe corner. It's seeing the shift early and moving first.

For developers and technical leaders curious where software is heading, and where the value goes.

session.name: Harness First: Turning LLMs into Production-Ready Agents
session.details:
A model alone does not make an agent. To solve real problems reliably, the model needs a harness around it: tools, memory, context, workflows, guardrails, observability, and evaluation loops that shape how it reasons and acts. In this hands-on workshop, participants will start with a base LLM and progressively turn it into a production-ready agent by designing the surrounding system. We will cover how to define the agent’s task boundaries, connect tools and data sources, structure prompts and outputs, add human-in-the-loop controls, and align the agent’s behavior with the intended business goal. The second half of the workshop focuses on evaluation and iteration. Participants will learn how to build golden test sets, evaluate action paths, identify failure modes, debug unreliable behavior, and improve the harness through targeted changes rather than random prompt tweaking.

By the end, attendees will understand how to move beyond “it worked in the demo” and build agents that can be tested, aligned, monitored, and improved over time.

session.name: From Answering to Acting: Engineering Reliable Autonomous Enterprise Agents
session.details:
This session is the second part of the journey and begins where “Context Engineering Is the New Prompt Engineering” ends. Once an agent’s context is selected, secured, fresh, attributable, and validated, the next question is whether it can safely be allowed to act.

The session examines the controls required when agents move from generating answers to executing actions. It covers bounded reasoning loops, explicit state, budgets for steps, tokens, time, and cost, as well as tool contracts, action-time authorization, reversibility, approval gates, failure containment, and trajectory-level evaluation.

The concepts from the first session continue on the action side: context budgets become action budgets, retrieval contracts become tool contracts, access permissions become authorization to act, and context provenance becomes a complete audit trail.

Together, both sessions provide an end-to-end architecture for engineering reliable, observable, and gradually autonomous enterprise agents.

session.name: Designing Effective Synthetic Decision Personas
session.details:
Adding more agents can make an AI system more capable, but it can also increase latency, cost, coordination overhead, and the number of ways the system can fail. The difficult engineering question is not how to connect multiple agents, but when they genuinely improve the result and how to organize their work effectively.

This talk explores that question through the development of Synthetic Decision Personas: AI agents designed to represent distinct roles and perspectives in complex enterprise decisions. A central part of the work is comparing simpler, moderately complex, and more advanced architectures, then evaluating whether each additional layer produces enough improvement in quality and reliability to justify its cost.

The second challenge is constructing the personas themselves. Reliable personas cannot come from role labels and prompts alone. The session will discuss how to validate that personas remain grounded in their evidence, behave consistently with their mandate, contribute genuinely different judgment, and improve as new decisions and outcomes become available.

Attendees will gain a practical approach to building agentic systems and Synthetic Decision Personas that are reliable, accurate, efficient, and cost-conscious, from selecting the right architecture to constructing, validating, and improving the personas that operate within it.

session.name: Run LLMs Locally
session.details:
LLMs are increasingly accessible, yet their deployment typically relies on cloud services that raise privacy, security and cost concerns for researchers, developers and end‑users. This talk will present a fully reproducible pipeline for running state‑of‑the‑art LLMs locally on commodity laptops equipped with integrated AMD GPUs and Ubuntu. The live demo will demonstrate how to run models like Qwen, Gemma and Mellum locally with competitive latency and memory usage on a single machine with 32 GB RAM and an AMD Ryzen 7 cpu.
Key contributions of the talk include:
1. Hardware‑software co‑design: detailed requirements (kernel version, GTT configuration, driver flags) and a step‑by‑step guide to enable direct GPU memory access via RADV and the Linux kernel.
2. Inference workflow: end‑to‑end instructions for downloading pre‑quantized GGUF models, launching llama‑server, and interacting through a web UI or OpenAI‑compatible API endpoints.
3. Performance evaluation: Demo with benchmark results (latency, throughput, memory footprint), illustrating the trade‑offs between model size, precision, and GTT memory.
4. Security: Prompt Injection example, prevention strategies
Audience members will leave with a ready‑to‑run setup, scripts, and understanding of how to harness their own hardware for secure, cost‑effective LLM inference. (Disclaimer: this abstract was generated locally with GPT-OSS 20B, running at 18.9 tokens/sec).

session.name: Running Agents Locally with Open Source: From Laptop to Kubernetes
session.details:
AI agents are everywhere, but most developers are building on top of proprietary APIs, paying per token, and hoping their sensitive data doesn't end up in someone else's training set. When things work, they work great. When you hit a rate limit, a price hike, or a data privacy wall, suddenly your production agentic application becomes a liability.

The good news? The open source ecosystem has caught up with the release of open source models like Qwen 3.5. You can now run fully capable agentic AI systems, locally, on your own infrastructure, and at scale on Kubernetes, without compromising on model quality or developer experience.

In this session, we'll build a working AI agent from scratch using an open source stack: Ollama for local inference, Podman to containerize the entire stack, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) to wire up tools your agent can actually use. Once it's working locally, we'll show the path to scaling it up onto OpenShift/Kubernetes, keeping the same architecture that worked on your laptop.

You'll leave knowing how to:
• Run open models locally with zero cloud dependency
• Build an agent loop with real tools using MCP
• Containerize your agent stack with Podman for reproducibility
• Deploy and serve agents on Kubernetes with confidence

session.name: Video Killed the Radio Star - UI is Dead, Long Live the Prompt Box
session.details:
The UI is dying. Within a few years — maybe months — the primary interface to most software will be a prompt box. When that happens, the application stack you've spent a decade building becomes invisible plumbing, and the agent calling it becomes the user.
That shift breaks almost every assumption baked into modern backends: REST endpoints designed for screens, auth flows that assume a human clicks "Allow," errors written for developers to debug, business logic scattered across UI state machines. Your services aren't ready to be talked to.
This talk shows how to retrofit an agentic layer onto existing backend services so they're ready when the UI disappears — drawn from a production system serving real traffic today. You'll leave with a concrete architecture, the patterns that worked, the ones that didn't, and a migration path that doesn't require throwing away what you already have.

session.name: Designing Production-Ready Agentic Systems: Lessons from the Field
session.details: Building AI agents that work in the real world requires more than smart models—it requires hard trade-offs, strict constraints, a lot of context engineering and disciplined execution. In this talk, we share practical lessons learned from designing and deploying verticalized agents in production environments, including voice-based systems where latency and responsiveness are critical. We discuss why unconstrained autonomy often fails, how introducing deterministic budgets for reasoning and tool usage improves predictability and cost control, and how artifact-based memory patterns reduce data exposure while increasing traceability. Drawing from our experience with real-time voice models, we explore strategies for managing latency, parallel tool execution, and streaming interactions without sacrificing reliability. This session focuses on concrete deployment challenges, common failure modes, and actionable guidance for building agentic systems that move beyond demos and consistently perform under real-world constraints.

session.longAbstract:
What to expect:

  • Ideation: A practical, hands-on methodology to come up with strong ideas that can be realized with the help of AI.

  • Refinement: Ideas are just that—ideas. In this part of the workshop we systematically surface failure points, edge cases, and operational constraints that typically only appear late in development

  • Testing your assumptions: Everyone ends up loving their idea, but until you actually build it, you’re relying on assumptions. In this part, we show you how to identify and test the critical assumptions that determine success or failure—reducing the risk of building something that never reaches usage.

  • Hands-on prototyping: You’ll build functional prototypes using a range of LLMs, compare outputs, and evaluate trade-offs in UX, reliability, and cost. The focus is not just on building—but on understanding what should (and should not) be built next.

  • Go home with a prototype and a methodology to validate your assumptions so you can get started for real with clear, actionable next-step plan grounded in engineering reality.

This is not just strategy, innovation, or yet another design thinking workshop—it’s real, hands-on product development in the era of AI focused on avoiding failure, making high-stakes decisions early, and ensuring your AI work actually reaches production and delivers impact.
session.name: AI Product Validation Day - From Idea to Validation
session.details: This hands-on workshop focuses on how to avoid wasted engineering cycles, de-risk decisions, and determine what is actually worth building before you commit resources. By the end of the day, you’ll leave with a working prototype, a validated set of assumptions, and a decision-ready case to justify (or kill) your project with confidence.

session.name: The Failure-to-Metric Method: Building Evals Your Platform Can't
session.details:
Building a custom eval metric is easy now; every platform lets you do it. The harder part, and the one that actually matters, is knowing which metric will serve your real business KPI.

I call this the Failure-to-Metric method. Start from a real production failure, not a benchmark. Decide if it's even worth a dedicated metric. If it is, design it around the moment things went wrong, not just where they ended up: did the system refuse when it should have, and how costly was the answer when it didn't.

I'll walk through how to recognize which failures actually matter and connect them to the KPI they're quietly damaging, using examples from high-stakes clinical workflows, where a wrong answer isn't just a bad user experience, it's a patient safety issue.

Then I'll show two metrics built this way. A Refusal Rate metric, scoring whether the system correctly declines to answer when it should (higher is better). A Hallucination Specificity Score, scoring how dangerous the answer was when it didn't refuse (lower is better).

You'll leave with the method, two working examples, and a way to decide which of your own production failures deserve a metric.

session.details:
Gen AI is a game changer applied to many industries and businesses. How can we leverage Generative AI for anomaly detection? And what benefit can we extract by using GenAI in our setup?

In this session I will address these issues. I will introduce you to a whole powerful family of Models you might not have heard from. It might even surprise you to hear, all the big players are involved in this research, Google, Meta, Facebook, and more. It is a frontier too few people have heard of, yet it might give you the edge you were looking for.

Let me show you how you can use these models so you can implement anomaly detection in your company today!

session.name: Context Engineering Is the New Prompt Engineering: Practical Patterns for Reliable Enterprise AI Agents
session.details:
This session is the first part of a two-session journey from reliable enterprise AI agents to safely autonomous systems. It focuses on everything that enters the model’s context window.

Carefully optimized prompts cannot prevent agents from using stale data, crossing permission boundaries, or producing decisions that cannot be reconstructed. Prompts shape how a model reasons, but context determines what it reasons about.

The session presents practical patterns for selecting, securing, refreshing, validating, and observing context. It covers retrieval, token budgets, access control, data freshness, memory, provenance, validation, observability, and evaluation. Applying data engineering principles such as contracts, lineage, freshness guarantees, and testing makes agent failures measurable and diagnosable.

This reliable context layer becomes the foundation for the second session, “From Answering to Acting,” which explores what must be engineered before an agent can safely execute actions.

session.longAbstract:
Day 1: From Vibes to a Spec That Holds

Build the fun way, find where it quietly goes wrong, and fix it at the source.

You will work on:

  • Building a working app from a plain-language description, using the AI tool you already use

  • Spotting code that works but solves the wrong problem

  • Turning vague prompts into a lightweight spec - clear intent, explicit constraints, checkable "done when" criteria

  • Driving the same build from your spec, and comparing the results

  • Reading the difference between a spec that holds and one that drifts

Focus:

Stop guessing what the AI will produce. Say what you mean precisely enough that it builds the right thing with any tool.
session.name: Agentic Software Engineering Bootcamp Day 1: From Spec to Production-Ready Software
session.details:
Your AI assistant wrote the feature. The tests pass. It looks correct. But you didn't read every line, so how do you know it does what you meant? Maybe the model got it right the first time. Maybe not. From where you sit, those two outcomes look identical. That uncertainty, not the quality of any one tool, is the real distance between "I built something" and "I can put this in production."

This hands-on, two-day workshop closes that distance. Day one is about aim: build fast and loose, hit the moment the assistant confidently produces something other than what you intended, and learn that the specification, not the code, was always the hard part. You'll leave with an app that does what you actually meant.

Day two is about confidence. You'll build your own pre-commit checks for quality, security, dependency vulnerabilities, and your own design standards, and wire them into a gate that blocks bad commits across the whole codebase.

For developers who already code with AI and want to move from "it works on my machine" to "I'd put my name on this." Bring a laptop and the AI tool you already use.

session.name: When Code Becomes Free: The Organizational Bottleneck of the AI Age
session.details:
What happens when code becomes nearly free to produce, time-to-market approaches zero, and a single engineer ships 20–30 pull requests a day with AI?

This talk explores a growing paradox: as AI removes technical bottlenecks, a new one emerges—human judgment and organizational speed. While teams are busy aligning in meetings, AI continues building—often the wrong things, but at scale.

Using examples from advanced teams (e.g. Boris Cherny, Claude Code), the session reframes software development in 2026: the challenge is no longer writing code, but making decisions fast enough to keep up. Build to think, not think to build. Ship variants, observe outcomes, and decide based on reality.

The real shift for leaders is not prompting—it’s designing decision architectures: turning alignment into infrastructure, decisions into deployed systems, and exploration into a disciplined practice.

For engineering, product, and executive leaders navigating the shift from building faster to deciding faster.

session.name: What gets measured gets optimized: evaluating the tools and skills your agents use
session.details: Everyone is shipping tools and skills for agents, but almost nobody can tell you whether theirs actually help. "It felt better in the demo" is not a metric, and with agents it is often wrong: something can look great in one transcript and quietly fail much of the time in aggregate. This deep dive shows how to put real numbers on the effectiveness and efficiency of agent-facing tools and skills. The order matters: effectiveness first, efficiency second, because saving cost is worthless if the agent never reaches the goal. Using real evaluation infrastructure as the worked example, I will cover how to run controlled with-and-without experiments scored against explicit checks, how to read the results to decide where to invest, an honest case where adding guidance made things worse, and the efficiency levers, and their trade-offs, that bring cost down once quality holds. You leave able to design an evaluation for your own agent tools instead of trusting a good-looking demo.

session.name: Agents don’t need more tools. They need architecture.
session.details:
Many agent prototypes start the same way: a model, a large prompt, lots of tools, and the hope that this will somehow become a product. At the latest, when tasks run for longer, users intervene, tools become risky, or multiple specialists are expected to collaborate, this pattern is no longer sufficient.

This session is about how to think about agent systems architecturally. We will discuss multi-agent patterns, supervisor agents, agent networks, tool boundaries, memory, handoffs, observability, and human-in-the-loop UX. Using Mastra as an example of agent orchestration and AG-UI as an example of user-agent interaction, we will show how individual agents can be turned into robust, traceable workflows.

The central question is: Where does collaboration between agents genuinely help, and where are we merely building a slow, expensive prompt conference?

Participants will learn how to design, test, and debug agent systems without losing control of the system.

session.name: Hack Me If You Can: Designing Unbreakable LLM Guardrails
session.details:
Organizations are racing to add generative AI to their applications, but LLMs introduce a new attack surface. Prompt injection, jailbreaks, data leakage, unsafe outputs, and violations of business policy cannot be solved with traditional security controls alone.

This keynote explores how to design effective, layered guardrails for GenAI systems, combining prompt-injection detection, content safety, business rules, and input/output controls. We’ll look at how guardrails fail, how attackers adapt, and how observability, red teaming, and continuous evaluation can make defenses stronger over time.

The goal is not to build an LLM that can never be broken, but an AI system that expects to be attacked and gets harder to break every time someone tries.

session.name: Fine-Tuning Is the Easy Part: Adapting Open LLMs for Your Domain
session.details:
Everyone asks which LoRA rank to use. Almost nobody checks what their run actually optimizes, and a fine-tune can finish cleanly while optimizing the wrong thing.

Fine-tuning open LLMs is deceptively easy: the parts that look hard, the LoRA math and the training loop, are well understood and thoroughly tooled. You follow the tutorial, the loss goes down, the run finishes without a single error, and the model still comes out wrong. Or the run never starts, and the out-of-memory error won't tell you why. What decides whether a fine-tune works is the machinery around the training step: how your conversations become tokens and which of them carry the loss, where your GPU memory actually goes, and whether your evaluation can be trusted.

This is a practitioner's tour of that machinery: when fine-tuning is the right lever and when prompting or retrieval serves you better; how chat templates and assistant-only loss masking really work, and how they break without an error message; LoRA and QLoRA demystified from first principles with the numbers that matter; why parameter-efficient fine-tuning still runs out of memory when the weight arithmetic says it shouldn't; and why your evaluation harness is harder to build than the fine-tune itself.

You'll leave knowing which knobs matter, which are folklore, and which quick, preventative checks catch silent failures before they cost you a training run.
